title: Chapter 10 Drill: Vascular Surgery and Transplantation

items.stem: Ten days after liver transplantation, a 49-year-old man has a coarse hand tremor, headache, serum potassium of 5.8 mEq/L, low magnesium, and a rising creatinine. Liver enzymes are normal, and the tacrolimus trough level is well above target. Which is the best management?
options: Reduction of the tacrolimus dose, with close monitoring of trough levels
Intensified immunosuppression with pulse steroids for rejection
Plasmapheresis for acute antibody-mediated rejection
Ganciclovir therapy for presumed cytomegalovirus infection
items.explanation: Tremor, headache, hyperkalemia, hypomagnesemia, and nephrotoxicity with a supratherapeutic trough indicate calcineurin inhibitor toxicity, which is managed by lowering the dose and rechecking levels, with attention to interacting drugs. Normal liver enzymes make acute rejection unlikely, so more immunosuppression or plasmapheresis would add harm, and nothing in the picture points to cytomegalovirus disease that would justify ganciclovir.

items.stem: A 63-year-old woman with metastatic pancreatic cancer has acute swelling and pain of the right calf. Duplex shows an occlusive popliteal vein thrombus. Her creatinine clearance is normal, and she has no bleeding lesions. Which treatment is most appropriate?
options: Aspirin alone, since cancer prevents anticoagulant response
Apixaban for three months or more, while cancer is active
Warfarin for six weeks, stopped when the swelling resolves
A caval filter placed in all patients with cancer
items.explanation: Cancer-associated venous thromboembolism is treated with a direct oral anticoagulant such as apixaban for at least three to six months and continued as long as the cancer is active, because recurrence risk is high. Aspirin is inadequate for treatment, and a short warfarin course ends protection while the thrombotic risk persists. Filters are for patients who cannot receive anticoagulation, not routine in cancer.

items.stem: A 79-year-old man is brought in with sudden severe back pain and syncope. Blood pressure is 82/50 mm Hg, heart rate is 120, and a pulsatile abdominal mass is palpable. Bedside ultrasound shows a 7.5 cm aortic aneurysm with free fluid. What is the best initial management strategy?
options: Resuscitation with crystalloid to a normal blood pressure before surgery
Computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis before any intervention
Immediate operative control with permissive hypotension
Beta blockade to a heart rate under 60 and later elective repair
items.explanation: A ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm with instability needs immediate operative or endovascular control. Resuscitation aims at permissive hypotension with a systolic pressure around 70 to 90 mm Hg and preserved mentation, because raising pressure to normal can dislodge the retroperitoneal clot and increase bleeding. Imaging delays control in an unstable patient, and elective repair is irrelevant to a rupture.

items.stem: Seven months after liver transplantation from a donor after circulatory death, a 55-year-old woman has rising cholestatic enzymes and pruritus. Doppler shows a patent hepatic artery and portal vein. Cholangiography shows multiple nonanastomotic intrahepatic strictures. Which complication is most likely?
options: Ischemic-type biliary strictures
Acute cellular rejection of the portal tracts
Late hepatic artery thrombosis with graft necrosis
Recurrence of an unrelated biliary malignancy
items.explanation: Livers from donors after circulatory death suffer warm ischemia before cold preservation, and they develop ischemic cholangiopathy with multifocal nonanastomotic strictures more often than livers from brain-dead donors. A patent hepatic artery excludes thrombosis, and acute cellular rejection causes elevated enzymes with a different picture on histology and no stricturing. Malignant recurrence does not fit the history.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man undergoes open repair of a Crawford type II thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm. On the first postoperative morning, he cannot move his legs but has intact sensation to light touch. Which measure is most likely to reverse the deficit?
options: Intravenous steroids at high dose for spinal edema
CSF drainage with an elevated mean arterial pressure
Reoperation to reconstruct the superior mesenteric artery
Observation for 48 hours before any intervention
items.explanation: Delayed paraplegia after extensive thoracoabdominal repair reflects spinal cord ischemia from loss of segmental feeding vessels and high cerebrospinal fluid pressure. Draining cerebrospinal fluid and raising mean arterial pressure increase spinal cord perfusion pressure and can reverse the deficit when applied promptly. Steroids have no proven role, a visceral vessel reconstruction does not treat cord ischemia, and waiting lets the injury become permanent.

items.stem: A 76-year-old man in the intensive care unit has septic shock requiring high-dose vasopressors and a recent cardiac surgery. He now has abdominal distension and pain. Computed tomography shows diffuse bowel wall thickening with patent superior mesenteric artery and vein, without free air. Which is the most appropriate management?
options: Emergency superior mesenteric artery embolectomy through a laparotomy
Immediate bowel resection of the entire small intestine
Vasoconstrictor reduction with intra-arterial vasodilator infusion
Systemic anticoagulation alone for suspected venous thrombosis
items.explanation: Nonocclusive mesenteric ischemia arises from splanchnic vasoconstriction during low flow states and vasopressor use, with patent vessels on imaging. Management is restoring cardiac output and volume, minimizing vasoconstrictors, and giving an intra-arterial vasodilator such as papaverine through a catheter, with laparotomy only for peritonitis or necrosis. Embolectomy fits embolic occlusion, resection of all bowel is premature, and anticoagulation alone does not address vasospasm.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man with diabetes and end-stage kidney disease has a nonhealing ulcer on the left great toe for two months. Pedal pulses are not palpable, and the ankle-brachial index is 1.52 because the ankle vessels do not compress. Which test best assesses perfusion of the foot?
options: Repeat ankle-brachial index after a ten-minute rest period
Segmental pressure measurement at the thigh and calf only
Venous duplex imaging of the great saphenous vein
Toe-brachial index with toe pressures
items.explanation: Medial calcification of tibial arteries in diabetes and kidney disease makes the ankle vessels incompressible and the ankle-brachial index falsely high or uninterpretable. Digital arteries are usually spared, so a toe-brachial index or toe pressure gives a valid measure of perfusion. Repeating the index after resting gives the same artifact, thigh and calf cuffs share the calcification problem, and venous duplex does not assess arterial inflow.

items.stem: A 60-year-old woman has a painful, shallow 4 cm ulcer above the medial malleolus with surrounding brown skin discoloration, lipodermatosclerosis, and ankle edema. Ankle-brachial index is 1.0. Duplex shows great saphenous vein reflux. Which is the best initial therapy?
options: Multilayer compression with leg elevation, and later saphenous ablation
Skin grafting without any treatment of the underlying reflux
Prolonged oral antibiotics for a presumed chronic infection
Arterial bypass to improve distal perfusion of the leg
items.explanation: Venous ulcers at the medial malleolus come from chronic venous hypertension, and compression therapy with elevation is the base of treatment, with healing in most cases. Once the ulcer heals or is controlled, ablation of refluxing superficial veins lowers recurrence. Grafting without correcting reflux fails, antibiotics do not treat venous hypertension unless infection is present, and a normal arterial index shows that bypass is unneeded.

items.stem: Three hours after successful femoral embolectomy for acute leg ischemia, a 58-year-old man has severe calf pain out of proportion to the examination, a tense swollen calf, and pain with passive dorsiflexion of the toes. Pedal Doppler signals are present. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Elevation of the leg and an increased dose of opioid analgesia
Repeat angiography to exclude a retained embolus
Application of a circumferential compression wrap
Four-compartment fasciotomy of the leg
items.explanation: Reperfusion after prolonged ischemia causes muscle swelling inside the closed fascial compartments, producing compartment syndrome. Pain with passive stretch and a tense calf are the key signs, and present Doppler signals do not exclude it because arterial flow persists until pressures rise very high. Treatment is prompt four-compartment fasciotomy. Elevation and analgesia mask the problem, a compression wrap raises pressure, and angiography delays decompression.

items.stem: A 57-year-old right-handed man with stage 4 chronic kidney disease is expected to need hemodialysis within six months. Vein mapping shows a cephalic vein of 3 mm at the wrist of the left arm and an adequate radial artery. Which access plan is best?
options: Tunneled internal jugular catheter as the long-term dialysis access
Autogenous radiocephalic fistula in the nondominant arm
Prosthetic upper arm loop graft as the first-line access
Femoral vein catheter that is replaced every month
items.explanation: An autogenous arteriovenous fistula, preferably distal in the nondominant arm, has the best long-term patency and the lowest infection and intervention rates, and it needs weeks to months to mature, so it should be created before dialysis is needed. Catheters have the highest infection and central stenosis rates, and prosthetic grafts are used when veins are unsuitable. Femoral catheters are temporary measures only.

items.stem: A 74-year-old man presents 36 hours after the onset of a cold, numb right leg. The foot is mottled and fixed, with tense, rigid calf muscles and complete paralysis of the foot. Arterial and venous Doppler signals are both absent. Which is the best management?
options: Emergent embolectomy through a femoral artery exposure
Catheter-directed thrombolysis over 24 hours
Primary amputation, since the limb is not salvageable
Anticoagulation alone with limb elevation and observation
items.explanation: Dense paralysis, muscle rigidity, fixed mottling, and absent arterial and venous Doppler signals describe Rutherford category III acute ischemia with irreversible tissue death. Revascularization would release myoglobin, potassium, and acid into the circulation and risk systemic collapse without saving the limb, so primary amputation is the treatment. Embolectomy and thrombolysis are for viable or marginally threatened limbs, and anticoagulation alone does not salvage dead muscle.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man has a 2.3 cm asymptomatic popliteal artery aneurysm found on duplex ultrasound done for a swollen knee. Duplex shows mural thrombus and runoff to two tibial vessels. Which is the most appropriate management?
options: Elective exclusion and bypass to prevent thromboembolic limb loss
Annual ultrasound surveillance until the aneurysm exceeds 5 cm
Aspirin alone, because rupture of these aneurysms is common
Direct puncture and coil embolization of the aneurysm sac
items.explanation: Popliteal aneurysms seldom rupture, but they threaten the limb through thrombosis and distal embolization, so repair is advised at about 2 cm in diameter or when thrombus is present. The usual operation is exclusion with bypass or endovascular stent graft. A 5 cm threshold for surveillance is for aortic disease and would let embolization occur. Antiplatelet therapy alone does not prevent limb loss, and coil embolization of the sac without revascularization risks ischemia.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman with intermittent claudication has symptomatic heart failure with a reduced ejection fraction of 30 percent. Her physician is selecting medical therapy to improve walking distance and to reduce cardiovascular risk. Which drug should be avoided?
options: Atorvastatin to lower low-density lipoprotein cholesterol
Cilostazol
Low-dose aspirin for secondary cardiovascular prevention
A supervised, graded walking program three times weekly
items.explanation: Cilostazol, a phosphodiesterase 3 inhibitor, improves claudication distance, but it is contraindicated in heart failure of any severity because drugs of this class have increased mortality in patients with reduced ejection fraction. A statin and an antiplatelet agent are recommended for every patient with peripheral arterial disease, and a supervised walking program is first-line therapy and carries no cardiac contraindication here.

items.stem: Minutes after removal of a right internal jugular central venous catheter from a sitting 66-year-old patient, he develops sudden dyspnea, hypotension, and a loud churning sound over the precordium. Oxygen saturation is 82 percent. Which is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Sit him upright and give a rapid crystalloid bolus
Obtain a computed tomogram of the chest before any treatment
Give a thrombolytic drug for a presumed pulmonary embolus
Left lateral decubitus Trendelenburg position and oxygen
items.explanation: Sudden collapse with a mill-wheel murmur after catheter removal indicates venous air embolism, with air trapped in the right ventricle outflow. Positioning the patient left side down with the head lowered keeps air in the apex of the right ventricle away from the pulmonary outflow, and oxygen helps resorb it, with aspiration through a central line if available. Sitting upright worsens entrainment, imaging delays care, and thrombolytic drugs have no role for a gas embolus.

items.stem: Seven years after open repair of an abdominal aortic aneurysm with a prosthetic graft, a 71-year-old man presents with massive painless gastrointestinal bleeding after a small sentinel bleed earlier in the week. He is now hypotensive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Ischemic colitis from loss of inferior mesenteric flow
Bleeding from a Dieulafoy lesion in the gastric fundus
Aortoenteric fistula between the graft and the third part of the duodenum
Diverticular bleeding from the sigmoid colon
items.explanation: Gastrointestinal bleeding in a patient with a previous aortic graft is an aortoenteric fistula until proven otherwise. A herald bleed often precedes massive hemorrhage, and the third part of the duodenum lies against the proximal suture line. Ischemic colitis causes pain and bloody diarrhea rather than massive bleeding, and other lesions are far less likely in this setting. Endoscopy and computed tomography are used, and urgent surgery follows.

items.stem: Within minutes of unclamping during a kidney transplant, the graft that was initially pink becomes mottled, blue, and flaccid, with no urine output. The patient is ABO compatible, and a retrospective review shows a positive crossmatch from preformed antibodies. What is the appropriate management?
options: Pulse steroids and observation for 48 hours
Intravenous fluid bolus and high-dose diuretics
Anti-thymocyte globulin and watchful waiting
Immediate removal of the graft
items.explanation: Hyperacute rejection results from preformed antibodies against donor antigens, causing complement activation, endothelial injury, and thrombosis within minutes to hours, and it is irreversible. The graft must be removed to avoid sepsis and systemic inflammation. Steroids and lymphocyte-depleting therapy act on cellular rejection and fail here, and fluids or diuretics treat prerenal causes, not a thrombosed graft. Crossmatch testing before surgery prevents it.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman has new hypertension of 175/105 mm Hg that is resistant to three agents. Serum creatinine is normal. Duplex and angiography show a string-of-beads appearance of the mid and distal right renal artery with a mildly small kidney. What is the preferred treatment?
options: Primary renal artery stenting with a drug-eluting stent
Right nephrectomy for the atrophic kidney
Percutaneous balloon angioplasty without stenting
Aortorenal bypass with a prosthetic graft
items.explanation: A string-of-beads appearance in a young woman is medial fibromuscular dysplasia, a nonatherosclerotic renal artery disease causing renovascular hypertension. Balloon angioplasty alone gives durable blood pressure benefit, and stents are reserved for dissection or failure. Nephrectomy removes a salvageable kidney, and surgical bypass is held for complex lesions or failure because angioplasty has low morbidity.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man who smokes cannot walk more than 150 meters without calf pain that resolves in a few minutes of rest. He has no rest pain or tissue loss. The ankle-brachial index is 0.68 on the right. Which initial treatment is most appropriate?
options: Immediate angiography with percutaneous angioplasty of the superficial femoral artery
Supervised exercise, smoking cessation, a statin, and an antiplatelet agent
Femoral to popliteal bypass with a reversed saphenous vein graft
Lumbar sympathectomy to improve collateral blood flow
items.explanation: Claudication without rest pain or tissue loss carries a low risk of limb loss, and the first step is medical: structured supervised exercise, smoking cessation, a statin, and antiplatelet therapy, which improve walking distance and reduce cardiovascular events. Revascularization is for lifestyle-limiting symptoms that fail this program, not the first step. Sympathectomy has no proven role in claudication.

items.stem: A 47-year-old man has a proximal deep vein thrombosis of the left femoral vein with a small pulmonary embolus. He has an active duodenal ulcer bleed with a hemoglobin of 6.8 g/dL requiring transfusion, so anticoagulation cannot be given. Which intervention is most appropriate?
options: Retrievable inferior vena cava filter
Permanent bilateral femoral vein ligation to prevent embolism
Therapeutic anticoagulation with close monitoring of hemoglobin
Compression stockings and early ambulation as sole therapy
items.explanation: An inferior vena cava filter is indicated for acute proximal venous thromboembolism when anticoagulation is contraindicated, as with active major bleeding. A retrievable device is chosen, and anticoagulation is started and the filter removed once the bleeding risk has passed. Giving anticoagulation to a patient with a transfusion-requiring bleed is unsafe, and stockings plus walking do not prevent embolization of a proximal clot. Femoral ligation is obsolete.

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman has an asymptomatic 80 percent left internal carotid stenosis found on screening duplex. She has hypertension controlled with medication, takes a statin and aspirin, and has a life expectancy beyond five years. The institutional perioperative stroke rate is under 3 percent. What is the best recommendation?
options: Medical therapy alone, because asymptomatic lesions are never repaired
Carotid stenting without distal embolic protection, in all cases
Carotid endarterectomy together with continued best medical therapy
Repeat duplex imaging in five years without any change in treatment
items.explanation: For asymptomatic stenosis of 60 to 99 percent, revascularization reduces long-term stroke risk when the surgeon has a perioperative stroke and death rate under 3 percent and the patient is expected to live more than about five years, and medical therapy continues. Saying that asymptomatic disease is never repaired ignores these trials, stenting without protection raises embolic risk, and a five-year interval for an 80 percent lesion is unsafe.

items.stem: A 56-year-old man has an acute type B aortic dissection with controlled blood pressure and no pain after initial therapy. Imaging shows no malperfusion, no rupture, and no rapid aortic expansion. Which is the most appropriate management?
options: Emergency open repair with graft replacement of the descending aorta
Immediate thoracic endovascular aortic repair on all patients
Liberalized blood pressure targets to protect renal perfusion
Beta blockade and blood pressure control with serial imaging
items.explanation: Uncomplicated acute type B dissection is managed medically with strict control of blood pressure and heart rate, usually with intravenous beta blockers and then oral agents, with surveillance imaging to detect late aneurysmal dilatation. Surgery or stent grafting is reserved for complications such as malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain, or rapid expansion. Liberal pressure targets would raise wall stress and worsen the dissection.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man with diabetes has gangrene of the forefoot with spreading cellulitis to the midfoot and an abscess in the plantar space. His femoral and popliteal pulses are palpable, and his general condition is stable. He walks with a cane at home. Which amputation level is most likely to heal?
options: Below-knee amputation
Transmetatarsal amputation of the forefoot
Through-knee amputation at the femoral condyles
Hip disarticulation of the entire lower limb
items.explanation: With infection and gangrene extending to the midfoot, a distal amputation will not provide enough viable, well-perfused tissue, so the level moves up. A palpable popliteal pulse predicts that a below-knee stump will heal, and preserving the knee joint allows prosthetic use and lowers energy cost. A transmetatarsal level is inside the infection, and higher levels sacrifice function that is unneeded when the popliteal supply is intact.

items.stem: A 29-year-old man with severe traumatic brain injury has a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 3, with fixed pupils and absent corneal, cough, and gag reflexes. He has been cooled to a core temperature of 33 C and has a midazolam infusion running. What must be done before an apnea test?
options: Perform the apnea test at once, because reflexes are absent
Rewarm to normothermia and allow sedatives to clear
Add a paralytic drug to remove any spinal reflexes
Declare death on the basis of the examination alone
items.explanation: Determination of death by neurologic criteria requires exclusion of confounders: core temperature at or above 36 C, adequate blood pressure, normal electrolytes and acid-base status, and no residual sedatives or paralytics that could mimic the examination. Hypothermia and a sedative infusion can suppress brainstem function and make the apnea test unreliable. Paralytics worsen the problem, and the declaration cannot rest on a confounded examination.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman who smokes has had three months of abdominal pain 30 minutes after meals, fear of eating, and a loss of 12 kg. Abdominal examination is benign, and upper endoscopy and colonoscopy are normal. Which is the best next study?
options: Barium enema with delayed films of the colon
Repeat upper endoscopy with random duodenal biopsies
Hepatobiliary scintigraphy with a fatty meal stimulus
Computed tomographic angiography of the mesenteric arteries
items.explanation: Postprandial pain, food fear, and weight loss in a vascular-risk patient indicate chronic mesenteric ischemia, which usually needs two of the three visceral arteries to be narrowed. Computed tomographic angiography confirms it and defines anatomy for endovascular or open revascularization. Barium studies and repeat endoscopy do not image the vessels, and a fatty meal scintigram looks for biliary dysfunction rather than vascular stenosis.

items.stem: Fourteen months after a deceased-donor kidney transplant on tacrolimus, mycophenolate, and prednisone, a 38-year-old man has fever, night sweats, and a 4 cm cervical lymph node. Epstein-Barr viral load is high. Biopsy shows a CD20 positive monomorphic B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder. What is the first-line management?
options: Increased tacrolimus dosing to prevent rejection during the illness
Reduction of immunosuppression with rituximab-based therapy
Immediate allograft nephrectomy with return to dialysis
Antibiotics aimed at tuberculosis for the necrotic lymph node
items.explanation: Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder is driven by Epstein-Barr virus under chronic immunosuppression, usually B-cell, and is first managed by lowering immunosuppression to allow immune recovery, with the anti-CD20 antibody rituximab for CD20-positive disease and chemotherapy if the disease is resistant to these steps. Raising immunosuppression feeds the lymphoma, graft removal is not first-line, and empiric antituberculous therapy ignores the tissue diagnosis.

items.stem: A 67-year-old man who smoked for 40 years asks his surgeon about abdominal aortic aneurysm screening. He has no symptoms and has never had imaging of the abdomen. His brother had a ruptured aneurysm. Which screening strategy is recommended?
options: Annual computed tomography of the abdomen beginning at age 50
Abdominal ultrasound only if he develops pulsatile abdominal pain
One-time abdominal ultrasound, since he is a man aged 65 to 75 who has smoked
Magnetic resonance angiography of the aorta every two years
items.explanation: Men aged 65 to 75 who have ever smoked should have a single screening abdominal ultrasound, which is sensitive, inexpensive, and free of radiation, and it reduces aneurysm-related death. A family history strengthens the case. Annual computed tomography exposes patients to radiation without evidence of benefit, waiting for symptoms means diagnosis at rupture, and magnetic resonance angiography is not a screening tool.

items.stem: A 69-year-old man has a transient episode of right hand weakness and slurred speech lasting 40 minutes, three days ago. Duplex and angiography show a 75 percent stenosis of the left internal carotid artery. He is a good surgical candidate. What is the best management?
options: Carotid endarterectomy within two weeks of the event
Elective endarterectomy delayed for three months after the event
Aspirin and observation, with repeat duplex imaging annually
Intracranial bypass to the middle cerebral artery
items.explanation: A symptomatic carotid stenosis of 70 to 99 percent benefits from revascularization, and the benefit is greatest when the operation is done early, ideally within two weeks of the event, because recurrent stroke risk is highest in that period. Delay for months forfeits that benefit, medical therapy alone is inferior for a high-grade symptomatic lesion, and intracranial bypass has no role in carotid atherosclerosis.
